desc: The Sundarbans is the world's largest mangrove forest, spanning the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers in West Bengal and Bangladesh. Covering over 10,000 km², it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the largest tiger reserve in India. The forest is characterized by salt-tolerant mangrove trees including the iconic sundari tree. It is home to the Bengal tiger, saltwater crocodile, estuarine dolphin, and numerous bird species. The forest protects coastal communities from storm surges and cyclones while supporting a unique ecosystem of tidal waterways, mudflats, and islands.
fact: It is the world's largest mangrove forest spanning 10,000 km² in the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta · It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the largest tiger reserve in India · It protects coastal communities from cyclones and storm surges · It is home to Bengal tigers, saltwater crocodiles, and estuarine dolphins

desc: The Western Ghats evergreen forests are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth, running along the western escarpment of India. These tropical rainforests receive over 2,500 mm of annual rainfall, supporting an extraordinary diversity of flora and fauna. The forests are home to over 7,000 species of flowering plants, 500 bird species, and numerous endemic amphibians and reptiles. The Silent Valley National Park in Kerala represents one of the last intact tracts of pristine tropical evergreen forest in the region. The forests are the source of major rivers and regulate the climate of western India.
fact: The Western Ghats forests are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth · They host over 7,000 flowering plant species and 500 bird species · Silent Valley represents the last intact pristine evergreen forest tract · These forests regulate the climate and river systems of western India

desc: The Deccan Thorn Scrub Forests cover large parts of the semi-arid Deccan plateau in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, and Maharashtra. This forest type is characterized by drought-deciduous thorny trees and shrubs adapted to low rainfall and extreme temperatures. Dominant species include acacia, babul, and ber trees. The forests support a unique assemblage of wildlife including the Indian bustard, blackbuck, chinkara, and wolf. These forests are under pressure from agriculture and urbanization but remain crucial for maintaining the ecological balance of the rain-shadow Deccan region.
fact: The Deccan Thorn Scrub Forests cover semi-arid regions of the Deccan plateau · They feature drought-deciduous acacia, babul, and ber trees · They support rare wildlife including the Indian bustard and blackbuck · These forests maintain ecological balance in the rain-shadow Deccan region

desc: The North-Eastern subtropical forests cover the Brahmaputra Valley and surrounding hills of Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, and Arunachal Pradesh. These forests include tropical wet evergreen, subtropical broadleaf, and temperate coniferous types. The region receives extremely high rainfall, with Mawsynram in Meghalaya being the wettest place on Earth. The forests are among the most biodiverse in Asia, hosting the one-horned rhinoceros of Kaziranga, the golden langur, and the white-winged wood duck. The region has vast bamboo and cane forests supporting local tribal livelihoods and a rich diversity of orchids.
fact: The Northeast subtropical forests cover the Brahmaputra Valley and surrounding hills · They receive extremely high rainfall, including the wettest place on Earth at Mawsynram · They host the one-horned rhinoceros in Kaziranga and the golden langur · The region has vast bamboo forests and a rich diversity of orchids

desc: The Himalayan temperate forests extend along the middle elevations of the Himalayan range from Jammu and Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh. These forests are characterized by coniferous species including deodar, blue pine, spruce, and silver fir, mixed with broadleaf oaks and rhododendrons. They occur at elevations between 1,500 and 3,500 meters and experience cool summers and snowy winters. The forests are home to the Himalayan black bear, musk deer, monal pheasant, and snow leopard. The Great Himalayan National Park and Valley of Flowers are important protected areas within this forest zone. These forests are crucial for regulating water flow to the major rivers of northern India.
fact: Himalayan temperate forests extend along the middle elevations from Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh · They feature deodar, blue pine, spruce, and silver fir with broadleaf rhododendrons · They are home to Himalayan black bear, musk deer, and snow leopard · These forests regulate water flow to northern India's major rivers
